stories.title_en: Carnegie Mellon is putting computer science courses on YouTube for free

comments.author: pcompeau
comments.text: Hi! I'm Phillip Compeau, I teach in Carnegie Mellon's Griffin School of Computer Science, and I run CS Learn, which launched today. We're releasing full semesters of lectures from current CMU computer science courses across a variety of topics, with one course premiering each day this week. More courses come in January. Yes, MIT got here 25 years ago :). What I'm excited about is how we're doing it: a few of our students built tools that automate a lot of the production work, so a small team can get a course out quickly and still have people review every lecture. We'll have lots more coming across a wide array of subjects. I'd love to know if there are topics you would like to see us cover!

stories.summary_ja:
・主な議論点
 Carnegie Mellon大学（CMU）が计算机科学の講義をYouTubeで無公開したことが話題になり、 community では、長年existentする开放教育の流れにおけるCMUの位置づけ、特にAI時代における基礎教育の重要性が議論された。また、動画の音声质量问题や、今後期待される科目についての要望が多数挙げられた。

・賛否両論
 動画の音声关于は、教授がマイクから離れる音声が途切れるなどの技術的不満が指摘され、制作体制の改善が求められた。一方で、無公開という形自体には肯定的な意見が大勢を占め、特にAIの基礎知識が「道具」としてのAIと「脅威」との差を分けると主張する意見が注目された。

・注目コメント
 CMUの卒業生が、自身が学習しているTianqi Chen老师的ML Systems科目と連動するとして喜び、更に統計学や分散システムなどの科目リクエストをしたコメントは、communityの具体的な関心の高さを示している。また、AIについて「T-shirtに収まるほど簡潔に表現された基礎の重要性」を強調するコメントは、現在の技術的トレンドを捉えた洞察として議論をリードした。

comments.text: It does have a certain nostalgia seeing these screenshots, sort of comforting interfaces. UX-wise it could have probably been done (a lot) better, but there was no such thing widespread as UX-specialists as we have nowadays. In a certain way Visual Basic was the 'AI' of easier software development, so it lowered the entry for people to start making things and having fun to be proud of what they could make. Quality was not the goal. I am currently working at a place where the previous developer passed away a few years ago, but he was a die hard Visual Basic developer for around fifteen years, he must have started with Visual Basic somewhere around 2007. I have to maintain his code base and rarely make some minor adjustments to it. The application does what is needs to do, but the code base is hell. And some of these applications have been rewritten from scratch three or four times in a timespan of fifteen years and still it is hardly readable. Ten levels deep of nested if-statements, semi human readable variables with funny 1337 coder names all over the place, functions having thousands of lines of code. I tried my best to understand some parts, but I gave up. I just throw Claude against it to let AI explain what the heck is going on in the code and also let Claude make fixes in it. In the meantime I am rewriting it in another stack (Java) also with the help of AI. I have been developing mostly Java for 25 years, but this year with agentic coding everything changed and AI is also a life saver to migrate away from Visual Basic.

stories.summary_ja:
・主な議論点
コメントでは、1997〜2012年のVisual Basic（VB）プロジェクトの多样性と「Raw」な創造性が称賛されています。特に、現在の完璧なUI/UX指向の開発とは異なり、技術を試し、遊ぶことから始まった当時の開発文化に懐かしさと賞賛の声が上がっています。VBが programming のentry barrierを下げ、许多の人が「品质」より「創造の喜び」を重視した点が評価されています。

・賛否両論
一方で、VBプロジェクトの技術的限界を指摘する声もあります。具体には、UXとして不十分な点、保守が極めて困難な「地獄」のようなコード構造（例: 深いネスト、変数名の乱れ、巨大な関数）が問題視されています。この「創造性」と「技術的負債」の間には明確な対立が見られます。

・注目コメント
特に注目すべきコメントは、VBを「當時のAI」と比較した点です。これは、二者ともに技術の門檻を下げ、広範な創造活動を可能にした点で共通しているという洞察です。また、現在のAIツール（例: Claude）を用いて、かつてのVBコードの解析や、他言語（Java）への移行を試みている実例が紹介され、歴史的開発と現代の技術が連動していることが示されています。

stories.title_en: Japan's Hometown Tax (2018)
stories.title_ja: 日本のふるさと納税 (2018)

comments.author: cloudbonsai
comments.text: This is a way weirder system than the name suggests. patio11 explains it in detail in the article, but the gist is: 1. You can contribute to rural areas in return for a tax credit, effectively allowing you to redirect a portion of your taxes to another town. 2. The most important quirk of the system is that you can choose any towns to contribute to. There is no requirement of previous residence or whatever. In fact, most people contribute to towns with which they have no personal connection. 3. This ended up causing tax competition among local goverments. Quite a few towns started advertising expensive "gifts" to contributers. It went so far that some towns got banned from the hometwon tax system. It was introduced with good intension, but resulted in a very inefficient tax system.

comments.author: pastage
comments.text: In Sweden rich counties pay a tax to poor counties, it is about 1500USD per person and year from a rich county. https://sv.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kommunala_utj%C3%A4mningssyste...

comments.text: Indeed. Good system, I send a portion of my taxes to my hometown in Shimane prefecture and get in return some of the goods from local farmers. I have always wished a similar system existed in America.

comments.text: > To the extent that taxpayers donate to their hometowns, Tokyo no longer freerides on the substantial public expenditures required to raise and educate internal migrants. This is really great idea and justice too. For decades, the countryside in every country have sent off their youngsters to work for the country's economy. The real unsung heros are the rural families who spend everything on their children education and well being, only to be separated from their loved ones. It's not just families that got impacted; the entire communities, villages and districts became devoid of young work force who prefer to move to cities. This was tolerated under the assumption that the cities provide better living conditions for the youngsters and the next generations. But cities survive in an ecosystem provided by the country side. Starve country side, you starve cities.

comments.author: walrus01
comments.text: > Tokyo, for its perspective, views the regions with the noblesse oblige that you would expect a cosmopolitan center of culture and learning to have with respect to their benighted country bumpkin cousins. I've met several French people from small coastal villages who now live in Paris and it's been interesting to see that their perspective on Paris is basically: a) The native Parisians think people from their area are country bumpkins. b) The people who live in their hometowns almost universally think that Paris is dirty, crime-ridden, too crowded, too noisy, too expensive, etc. It almost completely mirrors the attitude of certain small town Americans towards NYC or Chicago or LA.

stories.summary_ja:
この制度は名前が示すより遥かに複雑で、納税者による地方への寄付と税額控除の連動、居住地の制限がないという2つの核心的な特徴がある。これは地方自治体間の税収競争を招き、高額な「gift」を提供することで寄付を誘う地域が相次ぎ、一部が制度から排除されるに至った。意図した-goodな目的 had にもかかわらず、結果として非効率な税制と化したという批判が dominant である。

賛否両論の分かれ目は、制度の理念 versus 実態のずれである。賛成論は、地方の若流出や教育投資の無駄を是正し、東京などの都市が地方の負担で成り立っているという「free rider」問題を解決するとして支持する。一方、反対論は、競争が過熱し、税の実質的な再分配としての機能が损なわれたと指摘する。

注目コメントとして、都市と地方の相互依存関係に焦点を当てた洞察がある。地方が若者を都市に送り出している現状を「都市は地方のエコシステムによって成り立つ」と表現し、地方を衰弱させれば都市も存続できだと警告する。これは単なる税制問題ではなく、国全体の持続可能性に関する根本的な議論を含んでいる。

stories.summary_ja:
**主な議論点**
BugMeNotの閉鎖後、その機能を代替する方法として、コミュニティで盛んに議論された。具体的には、一時的なメールアドレスの生成サービス、DuckDuckGoのメールアドレス非表示機能、個人のドメインを活用したキャッチオール設定など、複数の代替手段が挙げられた。また、BugMeNot自体が「利便性」の面で優れていたことが評価され、その役割が追忆された。

**賛否両論**
賛否両論は明確には見られなかった。代わりに、BugMeNotが閉鎖した理由についての見解が分かれた。一部のコメントでは、不正行為者による悪用が网站の閉鎖を招いたという指摘がなされた。これに対し、他のコメントでは、単なる「時流の変化」や技術的な制約が原因であるという見方也有った。

**注目コメント**
特に注目されたコメントは、BugMeNotの設立者たちの成功ストーリーである。設立者たちは、BugMeNotの高いPageRankを活用してRetailMeNotを立ち上げ、巨額のアフィリエイト収入を上げた後、売却・上場という二度の成功を収めたという。この comments は、単なるパスワード共有サイトから、大きなビジネスへと成長した「最も印象的な自力起業の例」の一つであると評され、BugMeNotの歴史的意義が強調された。

stories.title_en: If an App Asks for Full Disk Access or System and App Protection Override
stories.title_ja: アプリがフルディスクアクセスまたはシステムとアプリの保護オーバーライドを要求する場合

comments.author: gbdubs
comments.text: This is a very poorly conceived API. If developers' use cases don't fit cleanly into Apple's (narrow) idea about how a hypothetical app should work, developers will continue to feel like they need to request these expansive permissions. A good filesystem permission API could include any of these which would make users WAY safer and enable developers to request far smaller scopes: - Allow the developer to specify the common location(s) that they need access to. Rather than having to have the user select the folder they want to grant access to, have the developer say "this app uses data in these 5 folders, do you want to grant that access" - so much clearer, and useful in cases where an app has to integrate with other apps through the filesystem. - Readonly access. Allow an app to read your files but prevent writes or deletes. - Time limited access. Allow some kind of access and allow the user to auto-expire it rather than having to remember it exists. - Allow for negative access (i.e. allow labels or tags on directories to mark them as sensitive and prevent access by default - browsers could do this for their cookie stores, `~/.ssh` could ship with it as a default, etc.) Apple could have used this opportunity to think through the question of "why do developers ask for filesystem access, and how can we allow legitimate usage through well scoped access controls", but instead they built a bad API that will (I would guess) not actually allow developers to be more judicious or achieve any of the user-safety benefits. Apple needs to learn to talk to (and listen to) developers.

stories.summary_ja:
**主な議論点**
コミュニティの議論の中心は、Appleの新しいAPI設計が「開発者の実際のニーズ」と「ユーザーのセキュリティ」の両立に失敗したという批判です。特に、全ディスクへのアクセス権を要求するappsの増加と、その権限が過剰であることがProblem視されています。

**賛否両論**
*   **批判側**: APIは開発者に「狭い範囲の権限要求」を強いるが、実際のファイル連携の必要性を考慮せずに設計された。結果、開発者は依然として広範な権限を要求せざるを得ず、ユーザーのセキュリティ向上に貢献しない。
*   **賛成側**: 多くのappsが不要な全ディスクアクセス権を要求している現状を是正する必要があり、この変更は開発者に権限の必要性を明確にさせる良い変更である。ユーザーが承認するポップアップは、かえって開発者に責任を問うものである。

**注目コメント**
最初のコメントが特に洞察的です。単なる批判にとどまらず、具体的な改善案を提案しています。例えば、特定のフォルダのみを指定する「スコープ指定」、読み取り専用の「Readonly access」、自動期限付きの「Time limited access」、甚至に機密ディレクトリをデフォルトでブロックする「Negative access」などです。これは、セキュリティと利便性を両立させる可能性のある、非常に現実的な設計提案です。

stories.summary_ja:
以下は、Hacker News のコメントに関する議論の要点の日本語要約です。

**主な議論点**
コミュニティの議論は、主に「光ファイバ」に関する広告表現の適切性と、ケーブルと光ファイバの技術的な実用差異の二つに分かれました。多くのコメントが、Comcastの「fiber-powered Wi-Fi」という表現が、末端までが光ファイバであるかのような誤解を招くとして批判しました。技術的な観点では、光ファイバは停電時の耐久性や電力効率が優れているという声が上がりましたが、実際のユーザー体験として、帯域幅と安定性が同等であれば、末端の物理回路の種類は重要ではないという意見もあった습니다。

**賛否両論**

comments.author: mike_hearn
comments.text: No big surprises here. Big outages at big firms seem to always look like this. The electricity industry has this notion they call a black start, where they bring the grid online from zero. It's a very difficult operation because you can't start a generator straight into an offline grid otherwise it gets hit with full demand and can't keep frequency in the right range, which can damage equipment. So they have to start by disconnecting all the loads and then bringing load blocks back in sequence, trying to roughly balance available generation with the size of the next block. In practice black starts are extremely rare, but they can happen after a cascading failure in which something causes some generating stations to trip, redirecting load onto the remaining stations which can't handle it causing them to trip in turn. The entire grid can collapse in just 60 seconds or so once that kind of runaway failure starts. This kind of outage is very analogous to a black start. A few servers get into trouble - maybe they're in a crash loop or maybe their caches are cold - the load balancers shift traffic onto the remainder which then can't handle the load either and so the failure cascades. Once a service is in this state sometimes the only remedy is to disconnect all load, bring the servers back to stability, then bring load blocks back online in small chunks, making sure to never hit anything with the full load immediately to ensure any caches or JIT compilers have time to warm up. It's the sort of thing that requires a bit of preparation because naive ways of doing it like just randomly dropping 90% of requests will yield a broken service for everyone. Ideally your LB can drop traffic by modulus of the session cookie or similar, so users are let back in atomically. Black starting a service is obviously quite hard to practice, but is probably something that sufficiently well resourced SRE teams should try once a quarter or so on a test cluster. I used to be an SRE at Google and although we regularly started up new clusters and moved traffic around between them, actually starting an isolated service instance entirely from scratch was never something we practiced. I remember in a few cases teams discovered devs had introduced circular dependencies by accident, i.e. starting service X required service X to already exist, or it depended on service Y that in turn depended on X. Sometimes you can only find these things by practicing.

このコメントスレッドでは、Microsoftの大規模なメール障害について、複数の視点から議論が交わされています。

### 主な議論点
 community で最も議論されたポイントは、この障害が「黒Start」と呼ばれる電力網の完全停止からの再起動に似ているという比喻です。サービスが複数のサーバーで障害を起こし、負荷が残りのサーバーに集中することで連鎖的に障害が発生する「カスケーディング障害」が起きたと指摘されています。この状態から回復するには、全ての負荷を切り離し、サーバーを安定状態に戻した上で、少しずつ負荷を戻していく「黒Start」のようなプロセスが必要だとされています。

### 賛否両論
議論が分かれた点は、障害の根本原因であるソフトウェア欠陥の修正ではなく、システムの負荷を減らすことで回復できる可能性があったかどうかです。一部のコメントは、特定のIP範囲から接続を制限するなどして負荷を制御し、追加リソースを投入することで、欠陥を修正せずにサービスを徐々に復旧できる可能性があると主張しました。これに対して、この方法では根本的な問題が解決せず、一時的な対策にすぎないという反論も見られます。

### 注目コメント
特に洞察のあるコメントとして、AIの役割についての疑問が挙げられます。MicrosoftがこのパッチをAIで開発・テストしたのかどうか、また、AIの活用が人間の知識と技術の「萎縮」を引き起こした結果、この大障害への対応が遅れたのかどうかが問われるべきだという指摘があります。また、criticalなインフラストラクチャでWindowsを使用していることに驚きを示すコメントも注目されます。

comments.author: johnbender
comments.text: > This allows us to (1) elide modelling the semantics of the high level programming language, we can instead model the semantics of the machine--presumably simpler semantics ISAs are pretty complicated and reasoning about programs in that context is hard which is why we have high level languages. > This distinction in terminology used to be a colloquially accepted notion, when we heard "CompCert is a formally verified compiler" or "seL4 is a formally verified microkernel" we assumed the authors did not verify vacuous or trivial properties, because the work of verification itself was held to a high standard that highly affected the reputation of the researcher. CompCert has also had extensive empirical evaluation to vet the theorems. Famously the CSmith paper ( https://users.cs.utah.edu/~regehr/papers/pldi11-preprint.pdf ) has this rather choice quote: > As of early 2011, the under-development version of CompCert is the only compiler we have tested for which Csmith cannot find wrong-code errors. This is not for lack of trying: we have devoted about six CPU-years to the task. The apparent unbreakability of CompCert supports a strong argument that developing compiler optimizations within a proof framework, where safety checks are explicit and machine-checked, has tangible benefits for compiler users. At my work we've extended this to CPU millennia. I hasten to add this of course doesn't rule out the possibility of poorly formed assumptions in the semantics etc (it's empirical after all) but it helps to build evidence that we have the theorems and semantic design right. More generally differential testing of this sort offers a possible way forward to build evidence in favor of theorem statements beyond expert examination. > Every discussion of formal verification must come with a list of caveats, a precise understanding of what is trusted, what is proven and what is not. Anyone that seriously participates in this work practices this. The whole community. More importantly this is precisely the point of writing down a theorem so that we can closely examine the assumptions. To abuse the CompCert example yet further it's now entirely possible to draw the envelope of assumptions, which are many for a non-toy compiler: https://arxiv.org/html/2201.10280v2 . Last note, I like the kiki bouba diagram if only because it evinces the problematic "round cow" assumption and how that doesn't pan out for real software.

comments.author: mjb
comments.text: > For any first-order universally quantified property of a program we can write as a property-based test, I think we will be able to generate proofs at the binary level, against architecture models that have themselves been validated by millions of hours of testing. The challenge of extending this to multi-threaded programs, distributed systems, [..] will be years more of work we must conduct across thousands of verification engineers and researchers. I expect the distributed and concurrent version of this will come more quickly. In fact, I would be willing to bet that by EOY 2030 the bar mentioned here of single threaded software will be met for multi-threaded and distributed systems under non-adversarial failure modes. This is significantly more aggressive than most in the field (and I'm field-adjacent at best), but given the rate of progress I think it's actually a rather conservative bet (the really aggressive bet would be "July 2027"). > The more "bouba" a piece of software or a given layer is, the harder it is to talk about what makes it correct. We can always talk about some correct attributes, but to talk about a uniform notion of correctness is not possible in my opinion. I largely agree with this, although I do think we're going to see more progress than expected in quantifying (and therefore verifying) usability and "look and feel" aspects of software. The risk is that this happens in a "narrow" way that forces all 'correct' software to look and feel the same, because that sameness correlates with the learned definition of 'correct'. > In solving these challenges, I think random testing and random exploration in general will prove to be invaluable tools. A test execution is a measurement, so it produces information about the real underlying system that we can leverage to falsify, harden and validate the models we use for verification. The verifiability of testing will continue to be a huge driving force of its adoption as well as a gateway into the rest of formal methods, and maybe it will even help us trust when we hear software is "formally verified" instead of wondering what was left out or when someone will find a bug in there. Strongly agree with this.

comments.author: nanolith
comments.text: Proofs are useful insofar as the formal specification is sound. The problem is that building a sound formal specification is the hard part, and it's not something that LLMs are going to be particularly good at. Yes, they can write a formal specification. But, is this formal specification sound? Is it usable? Is it applicable? Is it complete? This all requires human level reasoning and perhaps beyond to verify. Once you have a sound formal specification, building proofs that software follows this specification is actually fairly straightforward. LLMs aren't doing any magic here.

comments.author: skybrian
comments.text: When there's a language specification and everyone agrees to use it, it means that "should this code compile" has a clear meaning and so does "compiler bug." Perhaps having common packages containing shared specifications for other desirable properties will be the way to go? From the user's point of view, the tool should act like a linter. Where will trust come from? For a popular software project, it's from having a trusted team to maintain it and lots of people (and bots) watching them. The result would be that someone can use the linter without needing to verify much themselves. And sure, you should be able to write and prove your own, custom properties too, but hopefully it will build on shared definitions.

comments.author: Taikonerd
comments.text: > A great example of this is the recent "binary verification" approach, where instead of proving facts about the programs themselves, we prove facts about the compiled binaries of those programs. This is an interesting argument; I can see pros and cons here. I'm not a formal-methods guy, but I'd imagine the reason that you might want to prove facts about the programs themselves is that they encode higher-level information "for free" -- such as, this function returns a Person. IIRC, there was research into special compilers that would produce TAL: Typed Assembly Language. The idea was that TAL could carry annotations that would be helpful to provers.

stories.summary_ja:
・主な議論点
Formal Verification（形式検証）の本質的な課題は、証明の対象となる「形式仕様（specification）」の正当性と完全性にあるという community の広い合意。証明が完了しても、その土台となる仕様に欠陥や仮定が含まれれば、実際のソフトウェアの正しさを保証できない。この「何を trusted とするか」の明示が、形式手法の限界と有効性を決めるため、常に議論の中心となる。

・賛否両論
賛成派は、形式検証を「高レベル言語の意味論のモデル化」という複雑な問題を、「より単純な機械語の意味論」に置き換えることで実用化が進むと主張。CompCert の事例や、差分テスト（differential testing）を含む経験的評価を証拠に、実用上の便益を強調する。反対派は、LLM が形式仕様を生成しても、その「正当性・完全性」を判断する人間レベルの推論が不可欠で、LLM がその課題を解決できるとは思えないとして、形式手法の根本的限界を指摘する。

・注目コメント
「Binary Verification」のアプローチに言及するコメントが注目される。高レベルの型情報（Personなど）を直接扱うのではなく、コンパイル済みのバイナリに対して証明を行うこの手法は、証明の対象を現実の実行コードに近づけるという意味で、形式手法と実世界の乖離を縮める可能性がある。また、フォーマル手法を「リンター（linter）」に例えるコメントは、広く使われるツールとしての形式検証の役割と、信頼の源（信頼できる開発者と community の監視）を明確にした洞察的な比喩である。

stories.summary_ja:
### 主な議論点
この議論の核心は、大企業における技術スタックの統一（標準化）に関するものです。コメント著者らは、経験の豊富な複数のチームが長年培ってきた異なる技術スタック（PHP、Haskellなど）を、経営層が「AIに有利」という理由で、誰も使わないGoやNode+Reactへ強制的に統合することに反対しています。この「DRY（繰り返さない）」の名の下にされたこの強制は、teamsの知見や投資を無視し、実際の開発の遅延やCommunicationの壁を生むだけだと批判されています。

### 賛否両論
*   **反対派（強制統一への批判）**: 技術選定はbottom-upで行うべきであり、top-downの強制は創造性と効率を阻害する。自チームの問題は自らで解決した方が高速で、他組織に依存するより「繰り返す（Write Everything Twice）」方が現実的で効果的だという意見が大勢です。
*   **賛成派（部分的な標準化の必要性）**: しかし、UIコンポーネントなど特定の部分は、徐々に標準化することで、Application全体の見た目の不整合やバグの重複を防ぎ、長期的なメンテナンスの負担を減らすことは可能だという指摘もあります。これは「オールオ-nothing」ではなく、段階的に進めるべきだという立場です。

### 注目コメント
「WET: Write Everything Twice」というコメントが特に注目されます。これはDRYの逆の概念で、似たようなツールを最初は二つ作ってから、何を結合するかを検討すべきだというものです。これは、抽象化や共有ライブラリへの過度な依存を警戒し、実際の開発のニーズに沿って、必要以上に早期に共通化するのを避ける、現実的なアプローチを提唱しています。また、「a little copying is better than a little dependency」というGoのことわざが引用され、依存関係のリスク versus コピーベースの灵活性のバランスを重視する姿勢がうかがえます。

squirclesの「次元上の Older Brother（年上の兄弟）」である「sphube」が紹介され、これも優れた形状であると指摘されています（arXivの論文参照）。また、squirclesを実際の設計に応用するためのツールのデモが共有され、その開発状況（エッジケースの処理に苦労しているなど）が率直に报告されています。このように、実践的な試みと理論的な背景が結びついたコメントが目を引きます。

コミュニティでは、JPMorgan Chaseのシステム障害の原因とその影響、特に金融機関の基盤システムの脆弱性について活発に議論された。カード決済の停止、支店の閉鎖、ネットバンキングの停止といった具体的な影響が報告され、似たような事例としてヨーロッパのRevolutの障害が比較された。技術的要因として、データベースの障害やクラウドサービスの停止が疑われるが、大手銀行が依然としてCOBOLなどの古く信頼性の高いメインフレームシステムに依存している点が指摘され、その「レガシーシステムの頑丈さ」と「現代的リスク」の両面から議論された。

・賛否両論
銀行の公表内容に対する信頼性について意见が分かれた。一部のユーザーは、銀行が影響を最小限に見せようとするための発表を「嘘」と断じ、実際には深刻なシステム停止が起きたと主張した。これに対し、他のコメントでは、 Suchな障害が発生した際には、技術部門の優先度が最初に引き下げられるため、普段は目立たないシステムの基盤の重要性が浮き彫りになるという観点が示された。

・注目コメント
特に注目されたコメントは、大手銀行の基盤がCOBOLやIMSなどの古く信頼性の高いメインフレームシステムに依存しているという指摘である。このコメントは、現代の金融インフラが「信頼性の高い旧技術」と「現代的なリスク（例：ネットワーク、クラウド依存）」の狭間で抱えるジレンマを洞察している。また、銀行の公表を完全に信じないという現実的なアプローチを示すコメントも、コミュニティの共感を得た。
stories.editor_note: JPMorgan Chaseの技術的問題が米国の銀行のオンラインバンキングの遅延を引き起こす

stories.title_en: Spamhaus new email sender requirements in November
stories.title_ja: Spamhausが11月に新しい-email送信者要件を導入

comments.author: BLKNSLVR
comments.text: > Publish forward-confirmed reverse DNS for every sending IP > Every sending IP must have a reverse DNS entry pointing to a fully qualified domain name (FQDN). That hostname must, in turn, resolve back to the same sending IP address. This is known as forward-confirmed reverse DNS (FCrDNS). An IP with missing or mismatched reverse DNS is treated as suspicious and is one of the most common reasons for an IP to be considered for listing. I self-host an email server behind my ISPs connection, and so I do not own the IP address that I send mail from, therefore I can't satisfy the reverse DNS requirement.

comments.author: albertgoeswoof
comments.text: These techniques rely on it being hard (or at least long winded) to setup a domain and server properly, such that spammers (who are self selected to be lazy) won’t do it right and give up quickly. But with AI, it’s easy to get DKIM, DMARC, HELO etc. set up perfectly for almost no effort (maybe fcrdns is a bit more complex as it’s a manual process at most ISPs) I think we are in the end going to go back to it just being based on IP (v4) reputation, and this is all theatre.

comments.author: cowlevel
comments.text: Spamhaus is effectively a protection racket. However, these specific requirements are extremely reasonable.

comments.author: computer23
comments.text: Anyone else having their email blocked by Microsoft and Spamhaus? Microsoft Office 365 relies on Spamhaus and was blocking my email because the HELO on the mail server was mydomain.com instead of mailserver.mydomain.com. Once the problem was fixed, it took time for Spamhaus to re-scan the mail server and take the mail server off the block list. And it took more time for Microsoft to stop blocking mail. https://check.spamhaus.org/

comments.author: xmddmx
comments.text: Can someone clarify, do these rules apply only to people running their own mail transport? Or does it also apply to people sending mail through their mail hosting company (when that company is not Google or Microsoft). Specific example: I run servers "at home" that send mail through SMTP. I have forward DNS properly set up, but my reverse DNS is syn-123-123-123-123.res.spectrum.com My mail servers are, however, sending the mail through my mail host (DreamHost) and so I'm hoping that not having reverse DNS at home won't be a problem. Am I reading the Spaumhaus rules correctly?

stories.summary_ja:
・主な議論点：Spamhausの新要件、特に送信IPへのforward-confirmed reverse DNS (FCrDNS) 設定義務付けに対して、個人や小規模送信者による実施の難しさ、特にISPが配布するIPでは対応不可能である点が大きな議論の的となった。

・賛否両論：一部では「Spamhausは実質的な保護収益（保護賄賂）である」という強烈な批判がある一方、多くの参与著者により「これらの特定の要件は非常に合理的である」との賛成意見が示された。また、Microsoft 365がSpamhausのリストを参照してブロックしているという実態報告もalyzed。

・注目コメント：AIの普及によりDKIMやDMARCなどの設定が极易しくなり、Spamhausの要件がスパム送信者に対しての障壁としての効能が薄れているという指摘。将来的にIPレピュテーションのみに基づく方式に戻る可能性があるとの予測が示された。

stories.title_en: Mem Is Shutting Down
stories.title_ja: Memが閉鎖

comments.author: FinnLobsien
comments.text: My theory on this is that Mem existed in a weird middle ground: 1. Note taking as a mechanism to organize one's knowledge or learn things faster is (in my experience) largely useful because the process is manual. The linking between notes and conscientious note-taking is useful because it forces your brain to be attentive and resurfaces knowledge you may have forgotten. When AI does the connecting, you lose part of that, which the personal knowledge management crowd probably didn't fully connect. 2. ChatGPT memory, AI meeting recorders, and similar apps united the more utilitarian aspect of "remember stuff I need to know" in tools you use for direct work so you didn't need a separate AI note-taking app. - I do applaud the Mem team for making a genuine attempt at something genuinely interesting and new.

comments.author: dvt
comments.text: First of all, I really do think people got a bit carried away with the "ChatGPT, summarize this email" meme. AI really is a revolutionary technology, but low hanging fruit like note-taking, summarization, etc. are not even remotely a killer product. Second, I also think that (outside of search), we'll look at the chatting interface of today's AI tools in 5 years and laugh at how antiquated they seem. Finally, Obsidian (not to mention Apple Notes) is free. So to be competitive here, your value prop has to be an absolute home run. I'm never going to root against fellow entrepreneurs, but this just seems like a more pricy, maybe more stylish Obsidian (without all the plugin ecosystem? and you also need a browser extension?). Obviously, hindsight is 20-20, but if I were to release a productivity app today, I would do a few things: 1) Open Source it. Especially in the age of agents, people want to make sure that no shenanigans are being done with sensitive data, especially when it involves private notes. 2) Dual license it. Folks have done this since Red Hat, and I think dual licensing for personal & professional use (or have a revenue cutoff like Unreal or Unity) is the move. 3) Create a plugin ecosystem around it. I think the great thing about agents is that even non-technical folks can come up with stuff and vibe-code a plugin. Incentivize people to do this and build a community.

comments.author: mrweasel
comments.text: Nothing against Mem, or people trying to built something, but this will become a problem for the larger AI companies. Much of their current revenue is coming from smaller startups building product on top of e.g. ChatGPT. While useful, I question if these smaller players will survive, especially if they have to pay the actual cost of their token usage. On the other hand, OpenAI is releasing Dot, so maybe they'll just service those customers directly in the future, or at least some of them.

comments.author: NoboruWataya
comments.text: I don't really understand the variety and complexity of note taking apps that have emerged the last few years. Taking notes has to be the simplest thing in the world, why over-engineer it like this? I used to use Joplin, recently I've realised that a text editor + git gives me everything I need.

comments.author: tulo
comments.text: Nice that they gave a 60-day export window, though shutdowns like this are why I keep long-term notes in plain local Markdown/SQLite.

stories.summary_ja:
**主な議論点**
Memの終了について、コミュニティではその製品コンセプトの問題点と、AIノートtaking市場の現状が大きく議論された。主な論点は、1) 手動のノート取りが持つ認知的価値とAIの自動化の狭間でMemが位置づけられていたこと、2) ChatGPTなどの大規模AIや無料の競合製品（Obsidianなど）に差別化要素が不足していたこと、3) AIノートtakingは「キラー製品」ではなく、利用者来说既存ツールに統合されやすい安価な機能であるという认识。

**賛否両論**
議論の分かれ目は、AIがノート取りや要約などの「安価な果実」を truly disruptするかどうかにあった。一部は、AIは革命的だが、ノート取りのような用途では既存の無料ツールや大手AIの機能に勝つ必要があると主張した。他方、Memの試み自体を評価する声もあったが、その多くが競争力の欠如を指摘した。

**注目コメント**
特に洞察のあるコメントとして、起業家向けの助言が挙げられる。future proofな生产力APPを作成する場合、1) オープンソース化による信頼性確保、2) ダブルライセンスによる収益化、3) プラグインエコシステムの構築、という3つの要素が不可欠だと指摘された。また、大手AI企業（OpenAIなど）が下游のスタートアップを吸収または直接サービス化する可能性を懸念するコメントも注目された。

comments.author: liquid_oil
comments.text: Reading a post from 2012 like this it's shocking how quickly the ladder has been pulled up in all computer careers, but I suppose it's not as bad as the ladder pull from the dotcom bubble to 2012 where you could previously land a career "knowing HTML".

comments.author: sorentwo
comments.text: Marking this as 2012 would help. It’s a fun read in a nostalgic, pre-ai kind of way, where emphasizing that developers should use bcrypt wasn’t standard practice.

comments.author: bryant
comments.text: tptacek may disagree, but this needs an update considering how much has changed both with AI and the economies of scale AI brings to the discipline. I'm anticipating "the fundamentals are crucial," and as much as I want to agree, I think practical realities show us otherwise. We're at a point where all someone needs to know is how to AI-program-manage and how to glean enough about the discipline (or any discipline at this point) from AI to be dangerous enough in the field. To be a builder, breaker, or defender wearing any color hat of their choosing... that's it, really.

comments.author: smashandgrab
comments.text: I hire for incident response roles. Honestly, despite how much has changed this is still the way to do it for us. You need to be versed in many things and more importantly, interested enough to not feel entirely stressed out when things hit the fan. As for AI it’s been great for things like log review but those were already pretty low skill requirements. We haven’t had much luck past that.

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点は、2012年当時のセキュリティ入门の容易さと、現在の将其困难さの対比です。コミュニティでは、時代の変化、特にAIの登場が技師の役割や必要 skills に与える影響について議論が集中しました。

賛否両論の焦点は、基础知识是否依然重要です。一部は「基本が重要」と主張しましたが、他方ではAIの普及により、実際には基本よりAIを活用する実践力が重視される now と反論しました。

注目コメントは、インシデントレスポンスの採用担当者のものです。彼は、現在でも「幅広い分野に興味を持ち、緊急時に対応できる関心と適応力」が重要だと強調し、AIはログ解析などの低難易度作業に留まるため、人間の本質的な能力は変わらないと论述しました。
